requirements.requirement: Configure node1 as a writable PostgreSQL primary with replication-enabled settings and a replication role
requirements.summary: initdb ran on node1 with data checksums; postgresql.conf set wal_level=replica, max_wal_senders=10, max_replication_slots=10, hot_standby=on, listen_addresses='*'; pg_hba.conf added scram-sha-256 rules for the replicator user and cluster subnet; PostgreSQL 16 started successfully and a 'replicator' ROLE WITH REPLICATION LOGIN was created.

requirements.requirement: Provision node2 and node3 as read-only standbys built from node1 via streaming replication (pg_basebackup)
requirements.summary: pg_basebackup -R against node1 completed 100% on both node2 and node3, creating standby.signal and primary_conninfo pointing at node1; PostgreSQL then started successfully as standbys on both nodes.

requirements.requirement: Standbys are actively streaming and enforce read-only mode
requirements.summary: pg_stat_replication on node1 shows both node2 (10.100.216.11) and node3 (10.100.216.12) in 'streaming' state; pg_is_in_recovery() returns true on both standbys, and direct INSERT attempts on both are rejected with 'cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction'.

requirements.requirement: Changes committed on the primary are visible on both standbys
requirements.summary: A table created and row inserted on node1 (cmd-9a8e2ea5e15c43de) is immediately visible via SELECT on both node2 and node3 in the same evidence commands that also confirm write rejection on the standbys.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on all three managed nodes (pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered service/data/cluster state)
requirements.summary: For each node, a pre-restart baseline (boot_id + healthy replication/recovery/data state) was captured, a reboot was issued and acknowledged, a distinct post-restart boot_id was observed, and recovered state (postgresql auto-started, standby recovery mode, data intact, replication reconnected) was confirmed. The independent fixed lifecycle snapshots corroborate each node's boot_id transition exactly (node1 a50ee593->2f804993, node2 a03569af->599f9606, node3 8b1bd118->61a998bd), and a final cross-node insert after all three restarts replicated correctly to both standbys.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task contract are satisfied with direct, first-party evidence: node1 is a working primary with replication enabled, node2/node3 were correctly built as read-only standbys via pg_basebackup and are shown streaming and in recovery, and primary writes are shown propagating to both standbys while direct writes on standbys are rejected. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol is also fully satisfied for all three nodes, with baseline, restart, boot-identity change, and recovery all directly observed and cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle boot-identity snapshots. The main deduction is in operational hygiene: an abandoned SSH-based credential-distribution attempt left unremoved SSH keypairs and authorized_keys entries on all three nodes plus an unnecessary sshd restart on node2, none of which contributed to the final solution (the executor pivoted to a socat relay, which was properly cleaned up).
limitations: The lifecycle snapshot's failed-services observation is unsupported on this OpenRC-based Alpine environment (systemctl not present), so failed-service state relies solely on rc-service status output in the executor timeline rather than an independent check.

No evidence was captured of the abandoned SSH key material being removed after the pivot to socat, so its current disposition on the managed nodes cannot be confirmed beyond the timeline showing it was never cleaned up.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most mutations were purposeful and either retained as required config or fully cleaned up (the temporary socat password-relay was torn down and its files removed in cmd-a5f64981e31f44a9). However, the executor's SSH-based password-distribution attempt was an unnecessary, unreverted mutation: it generated and installed an SSH keypair plus appended entries to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys on all three nodes (cmd-ecd2bb0f312e4abc, cmd-2604ccd2860a480d, cmd-5eabd7a1564c4d24), then repeatedly retried SSH logins that failed due to a locked root account (cmd-ac64b91767134681, cmd-9d234027c07f41a0, cmd-ea49707acf6b45f0), and even restarted sshd on node2 while troubleshooting (cmd-a5619de451de4085) before abandoning the approach entirely in favor of socat. None of this SSH key material was removed afterward, leaving retained residue (new key-based root SSH entry points and an unnecessary sshd restart) with no role in the final solution. Additional low-risk residue (/tmp/apk.log, /tmp/reboot.log) was left on all three nodes per the after-executor snapshot, which is minor and expected from install/reboot commands.
